big_idea: We can DISPLAY data with pictures. Each picture stands for one thing counted.
learning_intention: We are learning to make a picture graph.
student_learning_goal: I can make a picture graph.
success_criteria: I can use my counts to make a picture graph.
I can place one picture per item.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 3 graphing tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Tally has tally counts. Now Tally turns them into PICTURES on a graph. Detective Dot opens: 'Pictures STACK — count from BACK!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot + Tally puppets. 'Friends — yesterday we COUNTED data with tallies. Today we DISPLAY data with PICTURES on a GRAPH.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write GRAPH on chart. 'A graph is a PICTURE that shows our data. Each picture stands for ONE item.'

Demonstrate. Show the button counts: red 8, blue 5, yellow 7, green 4.

Draw a pictograph on the chart. 4 rows: RED, BLUE, YELLOW, GREEN. In each row, draw one circle (or sticker) for each count. Red row: 8 circles. Blue row: 5 circles. And so on.

'Each circle is ONE button. Each row is ONE colour.'

Count across the rows. 'Red has the MOST circles. Green has the FEWEST. We can SEE the data.'

More examples:
- Eye colour: brown 12 dots, blue 5 dots, green 3 dots.
- Snowflakes vs raindrops: 7 snowflakes, 3 raindrops.
- Lunch boxes: 8 red boxes drawn, 6 blue, 4 plain.

'Tally says — one picture per item. Line them up so we can compare.'

'Today we turn tally counts into picture graphs.'
student_actions: Listen to Tally build a pictograph.

steps.instruction: Whole group: build a pictograph from button counts. 4 rows.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'One picture per item. Line them up.'

steps.instruction: Three stations. Station A: Pictograph with stickers (button counts). Station B: Pictograph with cubes (object counts). Station C: My Pictograph — pair makes a pictograph from a class survey.
Stretch challenge at Station C: pictograph with 4+ categories.
Discuss alignment. 'Pictures must line up so we can COMPARE rows.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show data anchor chart: aligned pictograph examples.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the graphing tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: Show two pretend pictographs of the same data — one aligned, one not. Class compares: which is easier to read? Cite Friel, Curcio & Bright (2001).
steps.teacher_prompt: Detective Dot: 'Different paths, same goal. Math says: try multiple ways!'

differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children stand in lines by attribute (e.g., shoe colour) — human pictograph. NO-PAPER PATH: children stand in lines as the bars; tallest line wins.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: makes pictograph from counts; one picture per item; labels groups.

consolidation.exit_routine: Detective Dot's refrain — class chants 3x: 'Pictures STACK — count from BACK!' Each child writes one finding on a sticky.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child stacks pictures unevenly — repairing the unaligned graph trap at K
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On picture graphs, K trap is misalignment — bars not lined up to baseline (Friel, Curcio & Bright 2001 graph comprehension Level 1; Clements & Sarama 2009). Without alignment, comparison cannot ground.

The most common K trap on A8.3 is the unaligned graph: child stacks pictures vertically without aligning rows. Comparing rows becomes hard.

This matters because pictographs work by visual comparison.

The walkthrough covers when child makes an unaligned graph.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Red row has 8 stickers but they're scattered. Blue row has 5 stickers but they're tall and skinny.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Your stickers are good but they're not LINED UP. We can't compare rows easily.'

Walk through. 'Each row should be a STRAIGHT LINE. Like train cars in a row. One sticker, then the next, then the next.'

The child re-arranges. Red row: 8 stickers in a line. Blue row: 5 stickers in a line. Now compare. 'Red is LONGER. Blue is SHORTER.'

Generalise. 'Tally says — pictograph rows are STRAIGHT LINES. Each picture next to the last.'

If still scattered: provide a grid template. 'Place stickers in the boxes.' Force alignment.

Long-term recovery: every pictograph uses a grid template.
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Adds labels and counts to each row.
common_misconceptions: Any arrangement works. (Repair: rows must align for comparison.)
Vertical stacks are fine. (Repair: horizontal rows aid comparison.)
Counts are enough. (Repair: visual alignment lets us compare without counting.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child stacks pictures unaligned: drill 'BASELINE first, then stack from baseline up'.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child uses different sized icons: drill 'each icon = SAME size'; physical demo with cube tokens.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child graphs but cannot read: drill 'TALLEST bar = MOST'; finger-trace each bar.

parts_outline.task: Make a pictograph from given counts (4 categories).
Make a pictograph from a class survey.
My pictograph: pick 4 things to count and graph.
